_doc:
Farhold's raw materials and the nodes they come out of (BUILDING_EXPANSION §1). Until now the only materials in the game came out of recycled gear; this file is the other half — the stuff you dig, fell, cut and skim off a wreck. Read by js/resources.js, and by js/refine.js for the names of things.

THE ONE DESIGN DECISION THIS FILE EXISTS TO SERVE: a node has a richness AND a distance, and the player has to weigh one against the other. A mother lode four hundred metres away can be worse than a lean seam behind the house, because every trip home is time you are not swinging. `haul` below is the maths that makes that real, and js/resources.js turns it into a single number per node — units delivered per minute — so the choice is legible before you commit to it rather than a regret afterwards.

What a node carries: `resource` (what comes out), `richness` (a multiplier drawn from `richnessBands`, printed to the player), `yieldPerSecond` (kind.baseYield x richness — what you actually get standing at the face), `amount` (how much is left) and a respawn timer. Nothing is infinite except water, and nothing stays dead except a wreck.
_materialsDoc: kind: ore|stone|wood|organic|fluid|gas|salvage|rare|refined|part|goal. `tier` is roughly which age of the base wants it. `weight` is how heavy one unit hauls — it scales the walk home, which is why stone is annoying and gold is not. `value` is a rough coin-per-unit so shops and quests have somewhere to start. `stack` is the carry limit per trip on foot, before a cart.

iron_ore.name: Iron Ore
iron_ore.desc: Rusty red rock. The backbone of every tool you will make.

copper_ore.name: Copper Ore
copper_ore.desc: Green-streaked and soft. Wire, fittings, and half of bronze.

tin_ore.name: Tin Ore
tin_ore.desc: Scarce, and useless on its own. The other half of bronze.

coal.name: Coal
coal.desc: Burns hot enough to melt ore. The first fuel worth carrying.

silver_ore.name: Silver Ore
silver_ore.desc: Bright in the rock. Wanted by smiths, jewellers, and anything that must not corrode.

gold_ore.name: Gold Ore
gold_ore.desc: Heavy and soft. Contacts, coin, and things meant to impress.

stone.name: Stone
stone.desc: The bulk material. Everything wants it and nobody wants to carry it.

rubble.name: Rubble
rubble.desc: Broken rock off a quarry face. Feed for the stonecutter.

clay.name: Clay
clay.desc: Wet grey from a riverbank. Brick, tile and moulds.

sand.name: Sand
sand.desc: Shore and dune. Glass, and the mould a casting is poured into.

flint.name: Flint
flint.desc: Sharp when struck. Fire, and the first blade you will ever make.

log.name: Log
log.desc: A felled trunk. Heavy in the arms, cheap at the sawmill.

resin.name: Resin
resin.desc: Bled from a cut trunk. Glue, pitch and waterproofing.

fibre.name: Plant Fibre
fibre.desc: Stripped stalks. Rope and coarse cloth.

reed.name: Reed
reed.desc: Cut at the water's edge. Thatch, baskets, and a passable arrow shaft.

hide.name: Raw Hide
hide.desc: Off something that objected. Tans into leather.

bone.name: Bone
bone.desc: Glue, handles, and the ash a kiln wants.

sinew.name: Sinew
sinew.desc: Dried tendon. Bowstrings and bindings that outlast rope.

grain.name: Grain
grain.desc: From a plot you dug. Slow, safe, and it does not fight back.

game_meat.name: Game Meat
game_meat.desc: Raw. Cook it or regret it.

water.name: Water
water.desc: Rivers, wells and rain catchers. Coolant, mortar, and most of refining.

ice.name: Ice
ice.desc: On a frozen world it is the only water there is. Melt it.

vent_gas.name: Vent Gas
vent_gas.desc: Skimmed off a ground vent by a collector. You cannot pick this up by hand.

crystal_raw.name: Rough Crystal
crystal_raw.desc: Snapped off a spire. Cuts into lenses, focusers, and the heart of a waypoint.

obsidian.name: Volcanic Glass
obsidian.desc: Black and murderously sharp. Blades and the cheap route to a lens.

sulphur.name: Sulphur
sulphur.desc: Yellow crust round a vent. Acid, powder, and the start of fuel.

saltpetre.name: Saltpetre
saltpetre.desc: Scraped from cave walls. Half of anything that goes bang.

salt.name: Rock Salt
salt.desc: Preserving, tanning, and the chemical bench's dullest input.

salvage_metal.name: Salvaged Metal
salvage_metal.desc: Worked metal off a wreck. Skips the smelting — which is exactly why wrecks run out.

scrap_plate.name: Scrap Plate
scrap_plate.desc: Hull sheet, already rolled. Cut it down or melt it back.

meteoric_iron.name: Meteoric Iron
meteoric_iron.desc: Fell out of the sky and cooled on the way down. Better than anything you can smelt.

copper_ingot.name: Copper Ingot
copper_ingot.desc: Drawn into wire, beaten into fittings.

gold_ingot.name: Gold Ingot
gold_ingot.desc: The wire that carries a signal you cannot afford to lose.

bronze_ingot.name: Bronze Ingot
bronze_ingot.desc: Copper and tin. The first alloy, and still a good one.

steel_ingot.name: Steel Ingot
steel_ingot.desc: Iron cooked with carbon until it stops bending. Everything structural.

charcoal.name: Charcoal
charcoal.desc: Wood burnt with no air. Hotter than wood, cheaper than coal.

ash.name: Ash
ash.desc: What a fire leaves. Leach it for lye rather than sweeping it out.

lye.name: Lye
lye.desc: Ash and water. The tannery wants it; so do your hands not.

slag.name: Slag
slag.desc: The rock the ore was hiding in. Crush it for road gravel or tip it.

tailings.name: Tailings
tailings.desc: What the washer rinses out. There is still metal in it if you can be bothered.

cut_stone.name: Cut Stone
cut_stone.desc: Squared block. The wall tool eats these.

brick.name: Brick
brick.desc: Fired clay. Furnaces are built of it and then make more of it.

glass.name: Glass
glass.desc: Sand, fired. Windows, flasks, and rough optics.

plank.name: Plank
plank.desc: A log, sawn properly instead of hacked.

rope.name: Rope
rope.desc: Twisted fibre. Everything you build needs some.

iron_dust.name: Iron Dust
iron_dust.desc: Crushed iron ore. Smelts better than rock, and washes better still. Dust keeps its metal — there is no such thing as generic dust, so there is a line for each.

iron_concentrate.name: Iron Concentrate
iron_concentrate.desc: Washed dust: half the rock gone, so a smelter gets half again more metal out of a load. That is what the water is for.

acid.name: Acid
acid.desc: Sulphur and water, carefully. Etching and leaching.

coolant.name: Coolant
coolant.desc: Keeps a refinery from cooking itself. It will not run without it.

reagent.name: Reagent
reagent.desc: The chemical bench's output and the refinery's appetite.

lens.name: Ground Lens
lens.desc: Glass or crystal, ground true. Optics and sighting.

focuser.name: Cut Focuser
focuser.desc: A crystal cut to hold a field steady. The waypoint core is mostly these.

machine_part.name: Machine Part
machine_part.desc: Gears, shafts, bearings. Every tier-three structure is a pile of these.

wire.name: Wire
wire.desc: Copper drawn out thin. Ten structures in the catalogue ask for it — and until round 13 nothing in the game made a single unit, which is the sort of thing a catalogue written before its supply chain quietly leaves behind.

concrete.name: Concrete
concrete.desc: Gravel, sand and water. Poured for the things that have to take a real load.

control_board.name: Control Board
control_board.desc: Copper and gold on fired board. What tells a machine what to do.

tempered_alloy.name: Tempered Alloy
tempered_alloy.desc: Steel taken further than a forge can take it. Hulls and drive housings.

composite_plate.name: Composite Plate
composite_plate.desc: Alloy laid over cloth and resin. Light, and it does not care about heat.

aether_cell.name: Aether Cell
aether_cell.desc: A charged crystal in a sealed case. Holds power far longer than it should.

blast_charge.name: Blast Charge
blast_charge.desc: Powder, packed. Opens a quarry face or a collapsed adit in one go instead of an afternoon.

ration.name: Cooked Ration
ration.desc: Hot food. Eaten, not stored forever.

lift_fuel.name: Lift Fuel
lift_fuel.desc: The last thing you make, and the thing you burn every time you fly.

ship_hull.name: Hull Section
ship_hull.desc: One of four. It will not fly without all of them.

ship_avionics.name: Avionics Rack
ship_avionics.desc: Four of four, and the only one that needs a rare element.

waypoint_core.name: Waypoint Core
waypoint_core.desc: Seat it in a pad and your base joins the network.

warp_core.name: Warp Core
warp_core.desc: The second act. Another world's rare element, and a lot of patience.

_rareDoc: Rare elements are NOT listed above one by one, because which ones exist is the universe's business, not Farhold's — universe/data/elements.json assigns 1-2 to each planet. js/resources.js reads a planet's `rare` keys and makes a `rare_seam` node kind for each, borrowing the element's own name and colour. This table is only the bits Farhold needs that the universe does not say: how a seam behaves.
_nodeDoc: A node kind. `baseYield` is units per second at the face at richness 1.0 with the right tool — multiply by the node's richness for what the player actually gets. `swingSeconds` turns that into a per-swing number for the held-tool interaction (yieldPerSecond x swingSeconds). `amountBand` is how much is in one node before richness. `respawnSeconds` 0 means it never comes back (a wreck, a meteor). `hardness` is the tool tier needed: 0 bare hands, 1 stone/iron tool, 2 steel, 3 powered. `handMinable` false means a structure has to take it — gas vents, per §1.14. `biomes` are worldgen biome keys; empty means anywhere on land — BUT `indoors: true` keeps a kind out of the open-air scatter (a deep vein is a dungeon seam, and one on the surface is a hardness-2 iron seam a new player cannot work and cannot get past), `placedOnly: true` keeps it out entirely because an event system puts it down by hand, and `fromPlanet: true` does the same for the rare seam the field places itself. All three are read by js/resources.js `kindsForBiome`.

ore_outcrop.name: Ore Outcrop
ore_outcrop.desc: A seam breaking the surface. The bread and butter of a young base.

deep_vein.name: Deep Vein
deep_vein.desc: Underground, and something is usually standing in front of it. Roughly twice an outcrop, which is what pays for the fight.

boulder.name: Boulder
boulder.desc: One rock. Breaks up, does not come back, and there are always more.

quarry_face.name: Quarry Face
quarry_face.desc: A cliff you can work at for hours. Heavy, slow to carry — the node that most wants a cart.

clay_bank.name: Clay Bank
clay_bank.desc: Cut out of a riverbank with your hands if you have to.
clay_bank._r14: R14: `nearWater` is honoured by createNodeField now, so a clay bank is on a bank. It was scattered evenly over six biomes before, which is why 'where do you find clay?' had no answer — and clay gates the furnace and the kiln, the first two machines in the game.

sand_bar.name: Sand Bar
sand_bar.desc: Shore or dune. Endless, but only where there is a shore or a dune.

tree.name: Tree
tree.desc: Felled for timber. Regrows over a few in-game days — §1.4 — so a clearing is a crop, not a scar.

fibre_patch.name: Fibre Patch
fibre_patch.desc: Stalks and reeds. Free, fast, and you will still run out of rope.

crystal_spire.name: Crystal Spire
crystal_spire.desc: Snapped off in flakes. Slow work, and the only route to a focuser.

obsidian_flow.name: Obsidian Flow
obsidian_flow.desc: Cooled lava and the yellow crust around it.

ice_field.name: Ice Field
ice_field.desc: On a frozen world this is the water supply. Melt it before you can drink it.
ice_field._r14: R14: dropped `seaIce` — a water biome, so every ice field placed there was deleted as `gone`.

water_source.name: Water
water_source.desc: A river, a lake, a well. The one node that never runs out.
water_source._r14: `lake` and `coast` are WATER biomes and createNodeWorld marks any node on water `gone` — so the one node that never runs out only ever existed in marsh. It keeps `nearWater: true`, which R14 finally made `createNodeField` read, so it still sits at the water's edge; it just sits on the DRY side of it now.

gas_vent.name: Gas Vent
gas_vent.desc: You cannot cup this in your hands. Build a collector on it — §1.14.
gas_vent._r14: R14: dropped `toxic` — it is not a World Forge biome key, so it never matched anything.

wreck.name: Wreck
wreck.desc: Worked metal without a furnace — the early shortcut, and it never comes back.

camp_scrap.name: Cleared Camp
camp_scrap.desc: What the bandits left. Another reason to clear one — §1.16.

meteor_site.name: Meteor Fall
meteor_site.desc: Still warm. Placed where a meteor actually lands (js/meteors.js), never scattered: it is hardness 2 and holds iron ore, so on open ground it reads to a new player as iron they cannot mine — and meteoric iron turning up in a field nothing fell on is the opposite of §1.15's 'worth walking to'.

rare_seam.name: Rare Seam
rare_seam.desc: Whatever this planet happens to hold, from universe/data/elements.json. Never respawns: a planet has what it has, and when it is gone you go somewhere else — which is §9.6's whole point.

_richnessDoc: How rich a node rolls. The player sees the band name and the multiplier before they commit — that is half the trade-off; the other half is how far they had to walk. Weights are relative, so most nodes are Fair and a Mother Lode is a small event.
_bandDoc: §1.19 — a low-band starter world has enough to leave and no more. `richness` scales every node's roll; `density` scales how many there are; `rareChance` is the odds a rare seam gets placed at all.

low.note: Enough to build a ship. Not enough to get comfortable.

high.note: Worth coming back for once you can survive here.

_respawnDoc: §1.20 — nodes come back so a base site does not go sterile, but they come back a little poorer each time, down to a floor. So the ground around your house stays workable forever and is never as good as walking out to a fresh seam. That tension is the same one the distance trade-off is about.
_haulDoc:
THE TRADE-OFF, as numbers.

Standing at a node you get `yieldPerSecond` units. Getting them home is the cost: you can carry `carry` units per trip and you walk at `walkSpeed` metres a second, so a node `d` metres from where you are stockpiling delivers

    delivered = carry / (carry / yieldPerSecond + 2 * d / walkSpeed)

units a second. That single number is what js/resources.js prints on every node, and it is why a Mother Lode across the valley can lose to a Lean seam behind the workshop.

The escape hatch is §8: put a store inside a logistics pole's reach of the node and the ore goes straight into the pool — `d` becomes zero and the rich node wins again. So the real decision is not 'which node' but 'which node do I move my base to', which is the decision worth having.

`loadPenalty` is how much a heavy material slows the walk home: walkSpeed / (1 + loadPenalty * weight). Stone is miserable to carry and that is on purpose.
_toolDoc:
Tool tiers gate the hard nodes and multiply the soft ones — §1's recommendation that hand-mining stays slow enough that a drill feels like a promotion. `tier` must be >= the node's hardness or you cannot work it at all.

`from` says where a tier comes from in the PLAYER'S terms. Farhold has no pick slot: the tier is read off whatever weapon you are carrying (js/main.js `toolTierFor`), and nothing on screen ever said so — which is why 'you need a Steel Tool' read as a dead end rather than as an instruction. js/resources.js prints this line with every refusal.

hands.name: Bare Hands
hands.from: nothing at all in your hands

stone_tool.name: Stone Tool
stone_tool.from: carrying a stone, bone or wooden weapon

iron_tool.name: Iron Tool
iron_tool.from: carrying an iron, bronze, copper or silver weapon

steel_tool.name: Steel Tool
steel_tool.from: carrying a steel weapon: forge Steel at an Alloy Forge from iron ingots and charcoal, then craft or buy a steel blade

drill.name: Drill
drill.from: a Drill built on the seam and wired to a generator, which needs no tool of yours at all
drill.note: The promotion: it works the node while you are somewhere else, and it never gets tired.
